source_metadata.title: Targeting PI3K/Akt signal transduction for cancer therapy

extraction_note: This source is a narrative review. Atoms represent assertions made by the review. Trial-level findings are tagged secondary_reported_result and must not be treated as primary-study atoms.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review examines PI3K/Akt pathway functions in cancer, the status of pathway inhibitors, and combination strategies with conventional cancer therapies.
The review describes aberrant PI3K/Akt activation in cancer through alterations involving PIK3CA, PTEN, Akt, TSC1, and mTOR.
PI3K converts PIP2 to PIP3, which recruits signaling proteins including Akt; activated Akt then phosphorylates multiple substrates.
mTOR is presented as a common downstream effector of Akt that integrates multiple signals supporting cancer progression.
Class I PI3Ks are heterodimers composed of a p110 catalytic subunit and a p85 regulatory subunit.
The four class I catalytic isoforms p110alpha, p110beta, p110gamma, and p110delta are encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3CG, and PIK3CD, respectively.
The review identifies PIK3CA as the class I catalytic isoform most commonly implicated by mutation in human cancer.
Class II PI3Ks comprise PI3KC2alpha, PI3KC2beta, and PI3KC2gamma and lack regulatory subunits, allowing activation as monomers.
The review distinguishes class II PI3Ks by their lipid products and describes sortins, small GTPases, and myotubularins as major downstream effectors.
Class III PI3K VPS34 is described as regulating autophagy and macrophage phagocytosis through multiprotein complexes.
The review identifies three mammalian Akt isoforms, Akt1, Akt2, and Akt3, with different tissue distributions and cancer-related functions.
Akt activation is described as downstream of RTKs and GPCRs, with PI3K-generated PIP3 promoting PDK1-dependent Akt activation.
The review identifies RTKs, Toll-like receptors, and B-cell antigen receptors among major upstream activators of PI3K/Akt signaling.
RTKs including EGFRs, VEGFRs, and FGFRs can activate PI3K signaling after ligand-dependent receptor activation.
EGFR-family signaling is described as activating PI3K/Akt and contributing to tumor growth, survival, and metastasis.
VEGF/VEGFR-2 signaling is described as activating PI3K/Akt and contributing to tumor metastasis and angiogenesis.
FGFR signaling is described as contributing to cancer metastasis, angiogenesis, and changes in the tumor microenvironment through pathways that include PI3K/Akt.
TLR signaling can activate Akt, and the review links TLR-driven PI3K/Akt signaling with cancer progression and treatment resistance.
B-cell receptor signaling is described as activating PI3K, particularly PI3Kdelta, and supporting B-cell survival.
GPCRs can activate PI3K/Akt signaling through Ras and class I PI3Ks and are linked to cancer-cell proliferation and survival.
PTEN is described as a tumor suppressor and negative regulator of PI3K/Akt signaling whose loss or mutation can promote pathway activation.
The review links PTEN function with control of tumor-cell migration and angiogenesis.
Akt signaling is described as promoting tumor-cell survival, proliferation, growth, and metabolism through downstream effectors.
The review distinguishes mTORC1 and mTORC2 and describes both complexes as important downstream nodes in PI3K/Akt signaling.
GSK3 is described as an Akt substrate whose Akt-mediated phosphorylation inhibits GSK3 activity.
The review links GSK3 with cancer-related growth and metabolism, including regulation of glycogen synthase.
FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4, and FOXO6 are identified as direct downstream targets of Akt.
Akt-dependent phosphorylation is described as regulating FOXO localization and activity, with consequences for proliferation, apoptosis, and metabolism.
The TSC1/TSC2 complex suppresses mTORC1 through Rheb, while Akt-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 can relieve this suppression.
The review describes PI3K/Akt signaling as interacting with the p53-MDM2 axis, including Akt-dependent effects that can reduce p53 tumor-suppressor activity.
The review describes bidirectional crosstalk between PI3K/Akt and RAS/MAPK signaling that can contribute to feedback activation and treatment resistance.
Akt signaling is described as promoting NF-kB activation through IKK-related mechanisms, linking PI3K/Akt signaling to proliferation and angiogenesis.
The review describes functional crosstalk between Wnt/beta-catenin and PI3K/Akt signaling in cancer and cancer stem-cell self-renewal.
The review presents PI3K/Akt signaling as a contributor to tumorigenesis through effects on survival, proliferation, metabolism, and other cancer phenotypes.
PI3K/Akt activation is described as supporting cancer-cell survival by regulating proapoptotic and antiapoptotic proteins.
Dysregulated PI3K/Akt signaling is described as a mechanism of resistance to multiple cancer therapies.
The review reports that the IGF1R/p110beta/Akt/mTOR axis can confer resistance to alpelisib in PIK3CA-mutant breast cancer.
The review links Akt pathway activation with increased PD-L1 expression and describes PI3K/Akt signaling as relevant to immune resistance.
PI3K/Akt signaling is described as promoting metabolic programs that support cancer-cell growth, including glucose uptake and glycolytic metabolism.
PI3K/Akt signaling is described as contributing to tumor angiogenesis through signaling involving Akt, VEGF, and endothelial-cell responses.
The review links PI3K/Akt signaling to invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and metastatic behavior in multiple cancer models.
PI3K/Akt signaling is described as regulating inflammatory and immune-cell functions that can shape cancer progression.
PI3Kdelta is described as a major PI3K isoform activated downstream of T-cell receptors and B-cell receptors.
The review describes the tumor microenvironment as including immune cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and signaling molecules that interact with PI3K/Akt signaling.
Cancer-associated fibroblast-derived factors including HGF are described as activating PI3K/Akt signaling and contributing to cancer progression.
The review proposes that targeting PI3K signaling in stromal or endothelial components alongside conventional therapies may have therapeutic potential.
The review groups PI3K inhibitors into pan-class I, isoform-selective, and dual PI3K/mTOR strategies and summarizes clinical-development status as of 2021.
Alpelisib is described as a selective class I p110alpha inhibitor and taselisib as another isoform-selective PI3K inhibitor.
The review reports that a phase III trial of alpelisib plus fulvestrant prolonged outcomes in advanced breast cancer but increased hyperglycemia, rash, and diarrhea.
The review reports that taselisib had greater activity in PIK3CA-mutant tumors but was associated with diarrhea and hyperglycemia.
The review summarizes several Akt inhibitors in clinical development, including MK-2206, GSK-2141795, GSK-2110183, AZD5363, and GDC0068.
MK-2206 is described as an allosteric pan-Akt inhibitor with reported combination activity in preclinical and early clinical studies.
The review describes first-generation rapamycin analogues and later mTORC1/2 or PI3K/mTOR inhibitors as strategies to suppress downstream pathway signaling.

The review argues that PI3K/Akt pathway inhibitors may be combined with growth-factor inhibitors, MAPK inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunotherapy to address pathway feedback and resistance.
The review describes PI3K/Akt inhibition as a potential radiosensitizing strategy, while noting that combination approaches require attention to toxicity.
The review describes PI3K/Akt pathway modulation as a potential way to alter immune-cell or tumor immune responses and support combination immunotherapy.
The authors conclude that PI3K/Akt pathway inhibitors have therapeutic promise but are limited by toxicity, feedback activation, resistance, and the difficulty of selecting effective combinations.
The review identifies hyperglycemia, rash, and other toxicities as common problems that can limit PI3K/Akt inhibitor use.
The authors argue that improved mechanistic understanding, biomarker selection, and rational combinations are needed to improve PI3K/Akt-targeted cancer therapy.
The work reports support from the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, and listed provincial or institutional grants.
The authors declare no competing interests.
The review reports an IC50 of 3 nM for GDC-0941 against p110alpha and p110delta in kinase assays.
The review reports that a phase I study enrolled 35 patients with advanced solid tumors receiving BKM120 and identified 100 mg/day as the maximum tolerated dose.
The review reports remission in 29% of heavily pretreated patients with PIK3CA-mutant tumors treated with alpelisib plus fulvestrant.

population.label: Heavily pretreated patients with PIK3CA-mutant tumors

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports a 36% response rate with taselisib among breast-cancer patients with PIK3CA-mutant tumors.
